### Problem `#173` (`Adv-1`): `[WC2016 / Luogu P4258 / UOJ #171]` 挑战 NPC (Challenging NPC)

> **Judge Links**: [UOJ #171](https://uoj.ac/problem/171) / [Luogu P4258](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P4258)
> **Constraints**: $T \le 30$ test cases, $N \le 3M$, $M \le 100$ ($N$ balls, $M$ baskets, so $N + 3M \le 600$ vertices), Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.

#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal

We must place $N$ balls into $M$ baskets (each basket $j$ holds at most $3$ balls) so that **every ball is placed**, and among all valid placements we **maximize the number of "half-empty" baskets that contain $\le 1$ ball**. Why does Bipartite Flow / MCMF fail? In an MCMF network, giving basket $j$ a $+1$ reward for having $0$ or $1$ ball and $0$ reward for having $2$ or $3$ balls corresponds to marginal step rewards $(+1, 0, -1, 0)$ for the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd ball — which is **neither convex nor concave** (the 2nd ball costs $-1$ while the 3rd ball costs $0$)! Whenever a degree reward has a parity or pair-breaking jump at capacity $2$ vs. $3$ on $V \le 600$, reach for the **3-Vertex Triangle Blossom Gadget** (Section 4.2).

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

Let $c_j \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ be the number of balls placed in basket $j$, with $\sum_{j=1}^M c_j = N$. We want to maximize:

$$\sum_{j=1}^M c_j + \sum_{j=1}^M [c_j \le 1] = \sum_{j=1}^M \big(c_j + [c_j \le 1]\big)$$

subject to all $N$ balls being matched ($\sum_{j=1}^M c_j = N$). Look at the table of $f(c_j) = c_j + [c_j \le 1]$:

| Balls in Basket $j$ ($c_j$) | $c_j = 0$ | $c_j = 1$ | $c_j = 2$ | $c_j = 3$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Target Gadget Matches $f(c_j)$** | $0 + 1 = \mathbf{1}$ | $1 + 1 = \mathbf{2}$ | $2 + 0 = \mathbf{2}$ | $3 + 0 = \mathbf{3}$ |

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (3-Vertex Triangle Blossom Gadget & Two-Phase Order)

1. Split each basket $j \in \{1, \dots, M\}$ into **three vertices** $b_{j,1}, b_{j,2}, b_{j,3}$.
2. For each ball $i$ that can go into basket $j$, add undirected edges from $i$ to **all three** vertices $b_{j,1}, b_{j,2}, b_{j,3}$.
3. Add a **single internal edge $(b_{j,2}, b_{j,3})$** inside basket $j$.
4. **Why This Realizes $f(c_j)$**: If $c_j \in \{0, 1\}$, the ball (if any) matches $b_{j,1}$ while $(b_{j,2}, b_{j,3})$ remains intact ($+1$ bonus match). If $c_j \in \{2, 3\}$, the second ball must match $b_{j,2}$ or $b_{j,3}$, breaking $(b_{j,2}, b_{j,3})$ ($0$ bonus match)!
5. **Mandatory Two-Phase Blossom Execution**:
   - **Phase 1**: Loop over all **ball vertices** $i = 1, \dots, N$ and call `bfs(i)`. If any ball $i$ fails to match, output `0` (or impossible) immediately!
   - **Phase 2**: Loop over all **basket vertices** $b_{j,2}, b_{j,3}$ ($j = 1, \dots, M$) and call `bfs(v)`. Because augmenting paths in Blossom never unmatch an already-matched vertex, all $N$ balls remain matched, and the total matching size $\nu(G')$ satisfies $\text{Ans} = \nu(G') - N$!

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Suppose $N = 2$ balls $\{u_1, u_2\}$ and $M = 2$ baskets $\{B_1, B_2\}$ where both balls can go into either basket:

- After Phase 1 and Phase 2, $u_1$ matches $b_{1,1}$ (with $(b_{1,2}, b_{1,3})$ matched internally) and $u_2$ matches $b_{2,1}$ (with $(b_{2,2}, b_{2,3})$ matched internally). Total matches $= 4$, so $\text{Ans} = 4 - 2 = 2$ baskets with $\le 1$ ball.
- **What Breaks If You Connect a Full Triangle $(b_{j,1}, b_{j,2}), (b_{j,2}, b_{j,3}), (b_{j,3}, b_{j,1})$?** Even with a full triangle inside $\{b_{j,1}, b_{j,2}, b_{j,3}\}$, at most $1$ internal edge can be matched when $c_j \in \{0, 1\}$, so a full triangle also works — **however**, if you run `bfs` on basket vertices *before* ball vertices without checking that all $N$ balls are matched, an isolated ball $u_1$ with no edges would leave $\nu(G') > 0$ even though no valid placement of all $N$ balls exists!

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Progressive Hints for Problem #173"}
- **Hint 1**: Write down the total number of matched edges inside basket $j$ (external ball edges + internal basket edges) when $0, 1, 2, 3$ balls enter basket $j$.
- **Hint 2**: Split basket $j$ into $b_{j,1}, b_{j,2}, b_{j,3}$ and add $(b_{j,2}, b_{j,3})$. Verify that $c_j$ balls can achieve $c_j + [c_j \le 1]$ matched edges!
- **Hint 3**: Always augment all $N$ ball vertices first (`for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) bfs(i)`), then augment the remaining basket vertices, and output `total_matches - n` along with `belong[i] = (match[i] - n - 1) / 3 + 1`.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete C++ Implementation Contract — Problem #173 (Two-Phase Blossom Gadget)"}
```cpp
void solve_case() {
    int n, m, e;
    cin >> n >> m >> e;
    // Vertices 1..n: balls; n + 3*(j-1) + 1..3: basket j slots
    BlossomSolver solver(n + 3 * m);
    for (int j = 1; j <= m; ++j) {
        int b1 = n + 3 * (j - 1) + 1;
        int b2 = b1 + 1, b3 = b1 + 2;
        solver.add_edge(b2, b3); // Internal bonus edge!
    }
    for (int k = 0; k < e; ++k) {
        int u, j;
        cin >> u >> j;
        int b1 = n + 3 * (j - 1) + 1;
        solver.add_edge(u, b1);
        solver.add_edge(u, b1 + 1);
        solver.add_edge(u, b1 + 2);
    }
    int matched = 0;
    // Phase 1: Match all N balls first (mandatory!)
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
        if (!solver.match[i]) matched += solver.bfs(i);
    // Phase 2: Match remaining internal basket bonus edges
    for (int v = n + 1; v <= n + 3 * m; ++v)
        if (!solver.match[v]) matched += solver.bfs(v);

    cout << (matched - n) << "\n";
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
        cout << (solver.match[i] - n - 1) / 3 + 1 << (i == n ? '\n' : ' ');
}
```

### Problem `#174` (`Adv-2`): `[CF 1045A]` Last Chance

> **Judge Link**: [Codeforces 1045A](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1045/A)
> **Constraints**: $N \le 5000$ weapons, $M \le 5000$ spaceships, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.

#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal

We have $N$ weapons of three types targeting $M$ spaceships:

- **Type 0**: Fires at $1$ spaceship from an explicit list $K_i$.
- **Type 1**: Fires at $1$ spaceship in a contiguous interval $[l_i, r_i]$ (requires **1D Segment Tree Out-Tree**).
- **Type 2**: Fires at **either $0$ or $2$** spaceships from a given triple $\{a_i, b_i, c_i\}$, where the triples of all Type 2 weapons are **pairwise disjoint**!

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

In standard Max-Flow, an edge $S \xrightarrow{2} w_i$ allows Type 2 weapon $w_i$ to destroy $0, 1,$ or $2$ spaceships in $\{a_i, b_i, c_i\}$. Why can we **relax** $\{0, 2\}$ to $\{0, 1, 2\}$ during Dinic and fix any degree-$1$ violation in $O(1)$ time afterward?

Suppose in the maximum flow, a Type 2 weapon $w_i$ pushes only **$1$ unit of flow** (say to $a_i$), while neither $b_i$ nor $c_i$ is matched to $w_i$. Could $b_i$ be completely unmatched in the maximum flow? **No!** If $b_i$ were unmatched, $S \to w_i \to b_i \to T$ would be a valid augmenting path, contradicting maximality of the flow! Therefore, both $b_i$ and $c_i$ **must already be matched by some Type 0 or Type 1 weapon** (since Type 2 triples are pairwise disjoint!). We can simply **steal $b_i$ from that Type 0/1 weapon** and give $b_i$ to $w_i$ (so $w_i$ now destroys $2$ ships $\{a_i, b_i\}$, while the Type 0/1 weapon drops from $1$ ship to $0$ ships), preserving the total number of destroyed ships!

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Out-Tree + Post-Flow Leaf Theft)

1. Build an Out-Segment Tree over spaceships $[1, M]$ with leaves wired $\text{leaf}_s \xrightarrow{1} T$ and internal edges $p \xrightarrow{\infty} lc, rc$.
2. Connect Type 0 weapons $S \xrightarrow{1} w_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{leaf}_s$ ($s \in K_i$), Type 1 weapons $S \xrightarrow{1} w_i \xrightarrow{1} h$ for canonical Out-Tree hubs $h \subseteq [l_i, r_i]$, and Type 2 weapons $S \xrightarrow{2} w_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{leaf}_{a_i}, \text{leaf}_{b_i}, \text{leaf}_{c_i}$.
3. Run Dinic. Then decompose the flow on the Out-Tree DAG to find which weapon $w_i$ actually hit each matched spaceship $s$. Finally, for any Type 2 weapon $w_i$ that only hit $1$ ship $a_i$, reassign $b_i$ from its current Type 0/1 owner to $w_i$!

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

Suppose Type 1 weapon $w_1$ covers $[1, 2]$ and Type 2 weapon $w_2$ covers $\{1, 2, 3\}$. If Dinic routes $w_1 \to 1, w_2 \to 2$ (and $3$ is also hit by $w_3 \to 3$), $w_2$ has degree $1$. Post-processing steals ship $1$ from $w_1$ and assigns $\{1, 2\}$ to $w_2$, leaving $w_1$ idle and $w_2$ with $\{1, 2\}$ (size $2$)!

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Progressive Hints for Problem #174"}
- **Hint 1**: Why can't a Type 2 weapon with $1$ unit of flow have an unmatched neighbor $b_i$? Because $S \to w_i$ still has residual capacity $2 - 1 = 1$, so $S \to w_i \to b_i \to T$ would augment the flow!
- **Hint 2**: How do you reconstruct the explicit matching pairs $(w_i, \text{ship})$ through the Segment Tree Out-Tree? Run a simple DFS/path-peeling from each Type 1 weapon $w_i$ with $f(S \to w_i) = 1$ down the Out-Tree edges with $f(u \to v) > 0$, decrementing $f(u \to v)$ by $1$ along the path to the leaf!
- **Hint 3**: After recovering `owner[ship]` for all ships, loop over Type 2 weapons; if `assigned[w].size() == 1`, pick one of its other two targets `x`, erase `x` from `owner[x]`, and assign `owner[x] = w`.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete C++ Implementation Contract — Problem #174 (Path Peeling & Type-2 Theft)"}
```cpp
// After Dinic max-flow on Out-Tree:
int find_leaf_and_decrement(int u, Dinic &dinic) {
    if (is_ship_leaf[u]) return ship_id[u];
    for (auto &e : dinic.adj[u]) {
        if (e.to != parent_or_rev && e.flow > 0) {
            e.flow--;
            return find_leaf_and_decrement(e.to, dinic);
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
// Post-processing for Type 2 weapons with exactly 1 assigned ship:
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    if (type[i] == 2 && hits[i].size() == 1) {
        int taken = hits[i][0];
        int steal = (triple[i][0] != taken) ? triple[i][0] : triple[i][1];
        int old_w = owner[steal];
        hits[old_w].clear();
        owner[steal] = i;
        hits[i].push_back(steal);
    }
}
```

### Problem `#175` (`Mas-1`): All-Edges Matching Classification (`可行边` & `必须边`) & Matching Matroid Basis (`CF Gym 102155 J` / Tutte Pfaffian Oracle)

> **Judge Link**: [CF Gym 102155 Problem J (Choosing Subsets)](https://codeforces.com/gym/102155/problem/J)
> **Constraints**: $N \le 500$, $M \le \binom{N}{2}$, Vertex weights $w_v \le 10^9$, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.

#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal

Given a general non-bipartite graph $G = (V, E)$ with $N \le 500$, we must either:

1. **Task A (All-Edges Classification)**: Determine for **every** edge $e = (u, v) \in E$ whether $e$ belongs to **at least one** maximum matching (`可行边`) and whether $e$ belongs to **every** maximum matching (`必须边`).
2. **Task B (`CF Gym 102155 J`, Matching Matroid Basis)**: Find a maximum-matching-saturable subset of vertices $S \subseteq V$ of **maximum total vertex weight** $\sum_{v \in S} w_v$.

Both tasks require algebraic reasoning on the **Skew-Symmetric Tutte Matrix $T(G)$** (Theorem 22.4) in $O(N^3)$ time over $\mathbb{F}_{998244353}$.

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

Let $T(G)$ be the $N \times N$ skew-symmetric Tutte matrix with random $x_{u,v} \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times$.

- **For Task B (Matching Matroid)**: By Tutte's Theorem, a subset $S \subseteq V$ can be covered by some matching of $G$ iff the row space of $T(G)[S, V]$ has full rank $|S|$ — that is, the rows of $T(G)$ form a **linear matroid** over $\mathbb{F}_p$ that represents the **Matching Matroid**! Therefore, we simply sort the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_N$ in **descending order of weight $w_v$** and maintain a **Linear Basis (Gaussian Elimination)** over the rows of $T(G)$, greedily inserting row $T_{v_i, *}$ if it is linearly independent of previously chosen rows!
- **For Task A (Feasible & Essential Edges)**: Let $r = \operatorname{rank}(T(G)) = 2\nu(G)$. Pad $T(G)$ with $d = N - r$ universal dummy vertices $w_1, \dots, w_d$ connected to all $v \in V$ with random weights to form an invertible $(N+d) \times (N+d)$ skew-symmetric matrix $\hat{T}$, and compute $B = \hat{T}^{-1} \pmod p$. Then:
  - $(u, v)$ is **Feasible (`可行边`)** $\iff B_{u,v} \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$;
  - $(u, v)$ is **Essential (`必须边`)** $\iff T_{u,v} \cdot B_{v,u} \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Gaussian Elimination & Matrix Inversion)

1. Generate $T_{u,v} = \text{rng}() \bmod (p - 1) + 1$ and $T_{v,u} = (p - T_{u,v}) \bmod p$ for each $(u, v) \in E$.
2. For `CF Gym 102155 J`: Sort vertices by $w_v$ descending; insert each row into an $N$-dimensional Gaussian basis `basis[col]`. Every vertex whose row successfully inserts into `basis` is chosen!
3. For All-Edges Classification: Find $r = \operatorname{rank}(T)$, append $d = N - r$ universal dummy rows/columns to build $\hat{T}$ of size $K = N + d$, invert $\hat{T}$ via Gauss–Jordan elimination to get $B = \hat{T}^{-1}$, and read off $B_{u,v} \neq 0$ and $T_{u,v} B_{v,u} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ in $O(1)$ per edge!

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

On $G = K_3 = \{1, 2, 3\}$, $\nu(K_3) = 1$, so $r = 2$ and we add $d = 3 - 2 = 1$ universal dummy vertex $4$. Every pair in $\{1, 2, 3\}$ can match with the remaining vertex paired to $4$, so $B_{1,2}, B_{2,3}, B_{3,1}$ are all non-zero (**all 3 edges are feasible**), while none equals $T_{u,v}^{-1}$ (**0 edges are essential**).

- **What Breaks If You Forget the $d = N - 2\nu(G)$ Dummy Vertices?** On $K_3$, $N = 3$ is odd, so $\det T(K_3) = 0$ identically (`T` is singular and cannot be inverted at all)! Even if $N$ is even, whenever $\nu(G) < N/2$, $T(G)$ is singular and must be padded with $d = N - 2\nu(G)$ universal dummies before inversion.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Progressive Hints for Problem #175"}
- **Hint 1**: Why do the rows of $T(G)$ represent the Matching Matroid? Because if $S$ is covered by a matching $M$, then $V(M)$ is an even-sized superset of $S$ where $\det T[V(M), V(M)] \neq 0$, meaning the rows of $S$ are linearly independent in $T(G)$!
- **Hint 2**: How do you find $d = N - 2\nu(G)$ before building $\hat{T}$? Run one Gaussian elimination on a copy of $T(G)$ to find its rank $r = 2\nu(G)$, then set $d = N - r$.
- **Hint 3**: Once $B = \hat{T}^{-1}$ is computed in $O((N+d)^3)$, `feasible(u, v)` is `B[u][v] != 0` and `essential(u, v)` is `1LL * T[u][v] * B[v][u] % MOD == 1`.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete C++ Implementation Contract — Problem #175 (Tutte Inverse & Matching Matroid)"}
```cpp
const int MOD = 998244353;
long long qpow(long long a, long long b = MOD - 2) {
    long long r = 1;
    for (; b; b >>= 1, a = a * a % MOD) if (b & 1) r = r * a % MOD;
    return r;
}

// Invert K x K matrix A mod 998244353; returns rank and writes A^{-1} into invA
int invert_matrix(vector<vector<int>> A, vector<vector<int>> &invA) {
    int K = A.size();
    invA.assign(K, vector<int>(K, 0));
    for (int i = 0; i < K; ++i) invA[i][i] = 1;
    int rank = 0;
    for (int col = 0; col < K; ++col) {
        int piv = -1;
        for (int row = rank; row < K; ++row)
            if (A[row][col]) { piv = row; break; }
        if (piv == -1) continue;
        swap(A[rank], A[piv]); swap(invA[rank], invA[piv]);
        long long inv_p = qpow(A[rank][col]);
        for (int j = 0; j < K; ++j) {
            A[rank][j] = A[rank][j] * inv_p % MOD;
            invA[rank][j] = invA[rank][j] * inv_p % MOD;
        }
        for (int row = 0; row < K; ++row) if (row != rank && A[row][col]) {
            long long factor = A[row][col];
            for (int j = 0; j < K; ++j) {
                A[row][j] = (A[row][j] - factor * A[rank][j]) % MOD;
                if (A[row][j] < 0) A[row][j] += MOD;
                invA[row][j] = (invA[row][j] - factor * invA[rank][j]) % MOD;
                if (invA[row][j] < 0) invA[row][j] += MOD;
            }
        }
        ++rank;
    }
    return rank;
}
```

### Problem `#176` (`Mas-2`): `[NOI2019 / Luogu P5471 / LOJ #3159]` 弹跳 (Bounce) & 2D KD-Tree / Manhattan Hub Synthesis (`AGC 034D`)

> **Judge Links**: [LOJ #3159](https://loj.ac/p/3159) / [Luogu P5471](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P5471) / [AtCoder AGC 034D](https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc034/tasks/agc034_d)
> **Constraints**: $N \le 7 \times 10^4$ cities, $M \le 1.5 \times 10^5$ 2D rectangle jump devices, **Memory Limit $128\text{ MB}$**, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.

#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal

In `[NOI2019] 弹跳`, each jump device at city $p_k$ can reach all cities inside a 2D axis-aligned rectangle $[L_k, R_k] \times [D_k, U_k]$ at cost $t_k$, under a **strict $128\text{ MB}$ memory limit**. In its companion `[AGC 034D] Manhattan Max Matching`, we must pair $N$ red points $(RX_i, RY_i, RC_i)$ with $N$ blue points $(BX_j, BY_j, BC_j)$ ($\sum RC_i \le 10^4$) to **maximize total Manhattan distance** $\sum (|RX_i - BX_j| + |RY_i - BY_j|)$.

- In `NOI2019 弹跳`, building a 2D Segment Tree of $O(N \log^2 N)$ nodes plus $O(M \log^2 N)$ explicit graph edges requires $> 500\text{ MB}$ and immediately MLEs! We must replace it with an **$O(N)$-node 2D KD-Tree** with implicit bounding-box pruning!
- In `AGC 034D`, building $N^2 = 10^6$ bipartite MCMF edges TLEs; we factor the 2D Manhattan norm through **4 Sign Hubs** (Architecture 6).

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic / Logical Representation

- **2D KD-Tree Bounding-Box Decomposition**: Partition the $N$ points recursively by alternating `nth_element` on $x$ (even depth) and $y$ (odd depth). Each KD-Tree node $u$ stores its exact bounding box $[xl_u, xr_u] \times [yl_u, yr_u]$ and uses strictly $N$ nodes in total! In a Min-Cut or Flow problem on 2D rectangles, $u \xrightarrow{\infty, 0} lc_u, rc_u$ forms an $O(N)$-node Out-Tree where any rectangle query attaches to $O(\sqrt{N})$ canonical KD-Tree hubs. Under `NOI2019 弹跳`'s 128 MB limit, we don't even materialize the query-to-hub edges: the priority queue pushes `(dist, rect_id)` and lazily relaxes the KD-Tree subtrees, skipping any node $u$ whose `min_val[u] <= d`!
- **4-Sign Manhattan Factorization (`AGC 034D`)**: Rewrite the Manhattan distance between red point $i$ and blue point $j$ as:

  $$|RX_i - BX_j| + |RY_i - BY_j| = \max_{s_x, s_y \in \{+1, -1\}} \Big[ (s_x RX_i + s_y RY_i) + (-s_x BX_j - s_y BY_j) \Big]$$

  Since we are **maximizing** total cost in Max-Cost Max-Flow, the $\max$ over the $4$ sign pairs $(s_x, s_y) \in \{+1, -1\}^2$ is chosen automatically by the maximum-cost flow!

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (KD-Tree & 4-Sign Hubs)

1. **For `AGC 034D`**: Create **just $4$ virtual hubs** $H_0, H_1, H_2, H_3$ corresponding to $(s_x, s_y) \in \{(+1, +1), (+1, -1), (-1, +1), (-1, -1)\}$.
   - For each red group $i$, connect $S \xrightarrow{RC_i, 0} R_i$, and for each $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ connect $R_i \xrightarrow{\infty,\; s_x RX_i + s_y RY_i} H_k$.
   - For each blue group $j$, connect $B_j \xrightarrow{BC_j, 0} T$, and for each $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ connect $H_k \xrightarrow{\infty,\; -s_x BX_j - s_y BY_j} B_j$.
   - Total vertices $= 2N + 6$, total edges $= 10N$!
2. **For `NOI2019 弹跳`**: Build the $N$-node KD-Tree over the $N$ cities in $O(N \log N)$ time. When Dijkstra pops a rectangle jump `[L, R, D, U]` with time $d$, recursively traverse the KD-Tree:
   - If `d >= tag[u]` or `[L, R] x [D, U]` is disjoint from `[xl[u], xr[u]] x [yl[u], yr[u]]`, prune immediately!
   - If `[xl[u], xr[u]] x [yl[u], yr[u]]` is completely inside `[L, R] x [D, U]`, update `tag[u] = d`, relax the point at `u`, and stop!

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexample

In `AGC 034D` with $R_1 = (1, 2)$ and $B_1 = (4, 0)$:

- The 4 paths $R_1 \to H_k \to B_1$ have weights:
  - $(+1, +1)$: $(1 + 2) + (-4 - 0) = -1$
  - $(+1, -1)$: $(1 - 2) + (-4 + 0) = -5$
  - $(-1, +1)$: $(-1 + 2) + (4 - 0) = \mathbf{+5} = |1 - 4| + |2 - 0|$
  - $(-1, -1)$: $(-1 - 2) + (4 + 0) = +1$
- Max-Cost Flow automatically routes through $H_{(-1, +1)}$ to pick the exact maximum $+5$!
- **What Breaks If You Use 4-Sign Hubs for MINIMUM Manhattan Matching?** If you want to **minimize** $\sum (|RX_i - BX_j| + |RY_i - BY_j|)$, Min-Cost Flow picks the **minimum** over the 4 hubs ($-5$ instead of $+5$), which equals $-|RX_i - BX_j| - |RY_i - BY_j|$! The 4-Sign Hub trick works **only** when maximizing Manhattan distance (or cutting in a dual formulation); for *minimum* Manhattan distance in 1D, you must use the **CDQ Bi-Directional Sorted Value Chain** (Architecture 4, Problem `#172`)!

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Progressive Hints for Problem #176"}
- **Hint 1**: Why does `NOI2019 弹跳` give a $128\text{ MB}$ memory limit? Specifically to fail $O(M \log^2 N)$-edge 2D Segment Tree graphs! An $N$-node 2D KD-Tree uses only $O(N)$ memory.
- **Hint 2**: In the KD-Tree traversal `apply_rect(u, L, R, D, U, d)`, always check `if (d >= sub_tag[u]) return;` at the very top of the function so each KD-Tree node is tagged at most once in increasing order of Dijkstra distance `d`!
- **Hint 3**: For `AGC 034D`, remember to negate the costs (`-cost`) and add Johnson potentials (or Bellman-Ford initial potentials) before running Dijkstra-SSP for Max-Cost Max-Flow!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete C++ Implementation Contract — Problem #176 (2D KD-Tree & 4-Sign Manhattan Hubs)"}
```cpp
// Part A: 4-Sign Manhattan Hub Compilation (AGC 034D)
void build_manhattan_hubs(int N, MCMF &mcmf, int S, int T) {
    int H[4] = {2 * N + 1, 2 * N + 2, 2 * N + 3, 2 * N + 4};
    int sx[4] = {1, 1, -1, -1}, sy[4] = {1, -1, 1, -1};
    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        mcmf.add_edge(S, i, RC[i], 0);
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k)
            mcmf.add_edge(i, H[k], INF, -(sx[k] * RX[i] + sy[k] * RY[i]));
    }
    for (int j = 1; j <= N; ++j) {
        mcmf.add_edge(N + j, T, BC[j], 0);
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k)
            mcmf.add_edge(H[k], N + j, INF, -(-sx[k] * BX[j] - sy[k] * BY[j]));
    }
}

// Part B: 2D KD-Tree Bounding-Box Relaxation (NOI2019 Bounce, 128 MB)
void relax_kdt(int u, int L, int R, int D, int U, long long d) {
    if (!u || d >= sub_tag[u] || xr[u] < L || xl[u] > R || yr[u] < D || yl[u] > U)
        return;
    if (L <= xl[u] && xr[u] <= R && D <= yl[u] && yr[u] <= U) {
        sub_tag[u] = d;
        if (d < pt_dist[u]) {
            pt_dist[u] = d;
            pq.push({d, -u}); // -u denotes city u
        }
        return;
    }
    if (L <= px[u] && px[u] <= R && D <= py[u] && py[u] <= U && d < pt_dist[u]) {
        pt_dist[u] = d;
        pq.push({d, -u});
    }
    relax_kdt(lc[u], L, R, D, U, d);
    relax_kdt(rc[u], L, R, D, U, d);
}
```

## 7. Pre-Submission Checklist (`FM-22` & `H-22` Audit)

Before submitting any Data-Structure-Accelerated Flow Graph or Non-Bipartite Matching solution, verify all six invariants:

1. **In-Tree vs. Out-Tree Separation (`H-22`)**: Did you keep $\mathcal{T}_{\text{in}}$ (bottom-up: $lc, rc \to p$) and $\mathcal{T}_{\text{out}}$ (top-down: $p \to lc, rc$) as strictly separate node sets? Never make a single segment tree bidirectional!
2. **Capacity Placement (`FM-22`)**: Are all internal edges inside your Segment Tree, Persistent Segment Tree, KD-Tree, or Binary Lifting table set to **capacity $\infty$ and cost $0$**? Finite capacities $c_k$ and costs $w_k$ belong exclusively on the unique query bridge $b_{\text{in}, k} \xrightarrow{c_k, w_k} b_{\text{out}, k}$ or on the $N$ leaf edges!
3. **Duplicate-Key Leaf Chaining (`主席树`)**: In `insert_pst(u, prev, ...)`, did you connect `dinic.add_edge(u, prev, INF)` so earlier items with identical coordinate-compressed keys are never orphaned?
4. **4-Sign Manhattan Direction**: Are you **maximizing** $|x_1 - x_2| + |y_1 - y_2|$? Remember that 4-Sign Hubs only work for $\max$; for *minimizing* $|a_i - a_j|$ with $j < i$, use **CDQ + 1D Bi-Directional Sorted Value Chain** (`#172`).
5. **Blossom Bridge & Two-Phase Ordering**: In Edmonds' Blossom `contract(u, v, b)`, did you set `pre[x] = y` before advancing `y = match[x]`? And in vertex-splitting step gadgets (`#173`), did you augment mandatory ball vertices **before** optional internal basket edges?
6. **Tutte Dummy Padding**: Before inverting $T(G)$ to classify feasible/essential edges (`#175`), did you pad $T(G)$ with $d = N - 2\nu(G)$ universal dummy vertices so $\hat{T}$ has full rank $N + d$?

## 8. Chapter Summary, Quarantined Templates & Bridge to Chapter 23

In this chapter, we learned how to break through the $\Theta(N^2)$ edge barrier in flow networks by factoring structured transition blocks through **Virtual Hub DAGs**, and how to cross the bipartite barrier into **General Non-Bipartite Matching** via the Tutte–Berge formula, Gallai–Edmonds decomposition, Edmonds' Blossom contraction (`带花树`), and the Randomized Skew-Symmetric Tutte Matrix $T(G)$.

### Quarantined Pure-Template Problems

The following problems are direct implementations of standard data-structure-optimized shortest paths or bare matching templates without new modelling reductions; we list them here for reference:

| Problem ID | Title | Reason for Quarantine |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CF 786B** | Legacy | Pure Dual 1D Segment-Tree (`In-Tree` + `Out-Tree`) + Dijkstra template without flow/cut modelling. |
| **UOJ #80** | 二分图最大权匹配 | Pure Kuhn–Munkres $O(N^3)$ template (covered in Chapter 13). |
| **UOJ #81** | 一般图最大权匹配 | Pure Weighted Blossom LP Dual implementation template. |

### Bridge to Chapter 23: Simulated Min-Cost Max-Flow (`模拟费用流`)

What if even an $O(N \log N)$-node Virtual Hub DAG is **still too slow** for Dinic or Successive Shortest Paths — for instance, when $N = 2 \times 10^5$ and we need to send $K = 10^5$ units of flow in $O(N \log N)$ total time? In **Chapter 23 (Simulated Min-Cost Max-Flow, Regret Greedy & Slope Convexity)**, we will go one step further: instead of building the Virtual Hub DAG and feeding it to a black-box MCMF solver, we will **maintain the residual graph's augmenting paths and back-edges directly inside heaps, segment trees, and WQS/Slope Trick data structures**, simulating the exact augmenting steps of MCMF in $O(N \log N)$!
